Instead, it identifies categories of orthotic/prosthetic devices and supplies that are **not covered**.

## Specifically not covered
NC Medicaid does **not** cover the following under the Orthotics & Prosthetics policy:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup or duplicate devices** kept on hand or placed at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as defined in the policy’s coordinating-care section  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.2 / 4.2.1)

The policy’s broader general rule also says a service is not covered if it is **not medically necessary**, is **experimental/investigational or part of a clinical trial**, or is furnished **primarily for convenience** rather than treatment need ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.1, reflected in the policy structure and coverage criteria).

## General criteria that must be met for coverage
For coverage, the policy requires that the orthotic or prosthetic item/service meet the general Medicaid coverage criteria, including:

- It must be **individualized, specific, and consistent with the symptoms or confirmed diagnosis** of the illness or injury being treated
- It must **not exceed the beneficiary’s needs**
- It must be able to be **safely furnished**
- There must be **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**
- It must **not be furnished primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.1)

In addition, the policy requires that orthotics/prosthetics:

- Be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- Be **medically necessary to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level**
- Be **appropriate for use in a non-institutional setting** where normal life activities occur
- Be supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering clinician within **6 months** before initiation
- Have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering clinician  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

The policy also says:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when required to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary when they **replace all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary needs the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**
- Devices must be a **reasonable and medically necessary part of the treatment plan**, **consistent with the diagnosis and functional limitations**, and **of high quality with replacement parts available**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

## Bottom line
A device under Policy 5B is generally covered only if it is a medically necessary orthotic or prosthetic item ordered by an appropriate clinician, tied to the beneficiary’s diagnosis and functional needs, safe and cost-appropriate, and not primarily for convenience. It is specifically not covered if it is for comfort/convenience, a backup/duplicate, for nursing facility residents, covered elsewhere, or for hospice beneficiaries.  
([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), §§ 3.1, 3.2.1, 4.2)

For **continued services**, the policy requires:

### First, at least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- The beneficiary’s functional gains are **tenuous**. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)]

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, but **additional goals are indicated** and supported by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress** toward meeting goals and the documentation supports that continued treatment is warranted. - The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wants the services**; or
- The beneficiary has **not improved despite treatment plan modifications** and needs a **more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards. - the beneficiary has a medical, cognitive, intellectual, or developmental issue that **would not benefit from outpatient treatment services**;

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the governing congregate-setting PCS policy and confirmed there are no amendments returned for the PCS congregate policy or the general PCS policy. I also pulled the key sections on eligibility, covered services, and assessment requirements. Next I’ll answer directly from those sections.## Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for someone living in an assisted living facility, but only if the person meets the congregate-setting PCS criteria.

Under NC Medicaid’s congregate-setting PCS policy, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who **resides in a licensed Adult Care Home (ACH)** or certain licensed group homes and meets the functional and medical criteria. An assisted living facility will typically fall within the Adult Care Home/congregate-setting framework only if it is a **congregate facility licensed by North Carolina** as described in the policy. [[State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 3.2.1]

### What must be true for coverage
The beneficiary must:

- have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition causing unmet need for assistance;
- need help with at least:
  - **3 of 5 qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
  - **2 ADLs where 1 requires extensive assistance**, or
  - **2 ADLs where 1 requires full dependence**;
- live in a qualifying licensed congregate setting;
- have needs directly linked to the documented condition;
- be under the ongoing direct care of a physician; and
- be medically stable, meaning the person does **not** require continuous nursing care, monitoring, or supervision by a licensed health professional. [[State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 3.2.1]

The policy also requires, among other things, that:

- the facility be safe and appropriately inspected,
- no other third-party payer be responsible for PCS, and
- no family/household member or other informal caregiver be available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those times. [[State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 3.2.1]

### What services are covered
If eligible, Medicaid covers PCS in congregate settings including:

- hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs,
- related cueing/prompting/guiding when part of hands-on ADL help,
- medication assistance tied to the condition,
- help with adaptive/assistive devices or durable medical equipment tied to ADLs, and
- certain special assistance/delegated medical monitoring tasks. [[State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 3.3]

### Assessment/approval requirements
Eligibility and service level must be determined through a PCS assessment by **independent assessors** using NC Medicaid’s standardized process. For new admissions, the assessment must be **face-to-face in the congregate facility**, and physician attestation of medical necessity is required. [[State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 5.4.3]

## Bottom line
**Yes, PCS may be covered for a Medicaid beneficiary living in an assisted living facility**, **if** the facility is a qualifying licensed congregate setting and the beneficiary meets NC Medicaid’s medical, functional, and assessment requirements. It is **not automatic just because the person lives in assisted living**. [[State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), §§ 3.2.1, 3.3, 5.4.3]

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under the federal HCBS waiver regulations, the waiver request must include the **assurances in 42 C.F.R. § 441.302** and the **supporting documentation in 42 C.F.R. § 441.303**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) is shown in the corpus as current, and I checked amendments for it; the knowledge base shows **42 CFR Part 441 as the current authoritative document with no listed amendments**.

### 1. The application must identify the waiver authority and any statutory requirements the state seeks to waive
Under **42 C.F.R. § 441.301**, a waiver request must include:
- the **assurances** required by § 441.302;
- the **supporting documentation** required by § 441.303; and
- when applicable, requests to waive:
  - **statewideness** under **§ 1902(a)(1)**,
  - **comparability** under **§ 1902(a)(10)(B)**, and
  - certain **medically needy income/resource rules** under **§ 1902(a)(10)(C)(i)(III)**.  
See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), **42 C.F.R. § 441.301**.

### 2. The state must show the waiver serves people who would otherwise need institutional care
The waiver request must provide that services are furnished only to beneficiaries whom the state determines would, **without the waiver services**, require the Medicaid-covered level of care provided in a:
- hospital,
- nursing facility, or
- ICF/IID, as applicable.  
It also must describe the target group and the services to be furnished. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), **42 C.F.R. § 441.301(b)**.

### 3. The state must give CMS the required assurances
Under **42 C.F.R. § 441.302**, CMS will not grant the waiver unless the state gives satisfactory assurances, including at least:

- **Health and welfare safeguards** for beneficiaries;
- **Adequate provider standards**;
- Compliance with applicable **state licensure/certification** requirements;
- If more than one target group is served, assurance the state can meet the **unique service needs** of those groups;
- Assurance that services are provided in **home and community-based settings** consistent with the regulation;
- An **incident management system** meeting the rule’s requirements;
- **Financial accountability** for waiver funds;
- Proper **evaluation and reevaluation** of beneficiaries;
- That beneficiaries are informed of **feasible alternatives** and may choose between institutional and HCBS services;
- That the state will comply with applicable **post-eligibility treatment of income** rules; and
- Critically, that **average per capita expenditures under the waiver will not exceed** the average per capita expenditures that would have been made without the waiver.  
See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), **42 C.F.R. § 441.302**.

### 4. The state must support those assurances with documentation
Under **42 C.F.R. § 441.303**, the state must furnish sufficient information to support the assurances, including:

- a description of the **health and welfare safeguards**;
- a description of the **records and information** that will support financial accountability;
- the state’s plan for **evaluation and reevaluation**, including:
  - who performs them,
  - how they are done,
  - the evaluation form used,
  - how the form compares to institutional placement evaluation tools if different,
  - procedures for written documentation,
  - procedures for periodic reevaluation;
- a description of how eligible beneficiaries will be informed of **feasible alternatives** and allowed to choose institutional or HCBS services;
- an explanation of how the state will apply **post-eligibility income/resource rules** for certain individuals eligible under the special income rule;
- an explanation, with supporting documentation satisfactory to CMS, of how the state estimated **average per capita expenditures**.

### 5. The application must demonstrate cost neutrality
A central showing is the **cost-neutrality demonstration** in **42 C.F.R. § 441.303(f)**. The regulation requires that:

> the estimated annual average per capita expenditure for waiver and other Medicaid services for waiver participants **must not exceed** the estimated annual average per capita expenditures that would have been made in the absence of the waiver.

The regulation expresses this as:
**D + D′ ≤ G + G′**, where the left side is waiver-participant costs and the right side is the projected cost of institutional and other Medicaid services without the waiver.  
See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), **42 C.F.R. § 441.303(f)**.

### 6. The state must identify the program size
The state must indicate the number of **unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve each year. That number becomes a cap on the waiver program unless CMS approves an increase by amendment. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), **42 C.F.R. § 441.303(f)(6)**.

So, in plain terms:

- **Federal statutory authority:** **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**.
- **What NC must demonstrate in the waiver application:** that the waiver population would otherwise need institutional care; that the state has adequate health, safety, provider, and administrative safeguards; that beneficiaries get person-centered HCBS and meaningful choice; and that the waiver is **cost-neutral** compared with institutional care, supported by the documentation required in **42 C.F.R. §§ 441.301–441.303**.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?

NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible resident occupying a nursing facility bed that Medicaid is reimbursing. - It must be **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- It must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- The **necessity for the leave must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- The **therapeutic justification for each instance** must be entered into the **resident’s health record**.
- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the absence.
- The facility may not receive any Medicaid revenue for that resident other than **reimbursement for the reserved bed** during the leave.
- The facility must **keep a cumulative record** of therapeutic leave days for audit purposes, and the resident must be marked on the **midnight census** as on therapeutic leave.
- Medicaid will **not reimburse leave days beyond the legal limit**. [Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8.

Therapeutic leave does **not** apply if the absence is for the purpose of receiving:

- **inpatient services**, or
- **nursing services provided elsewhere or at a different level of care in the current facility**,

Medicaid also does **not** reimburse ambulance transportation to the therapeutic leave site because that transportation is not considered an emergency. [Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the governing federal rule in 42 CFR § 440.70 and confirmed the current authoritative document for Part 440. Next I’ll answer directly from that section, focusing on the definition, the listed components of home health services, and the location rules/excluded settings.## Federal definition of “home health services”

Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary:

- **at the person’s place of residence**; and
- **under written orders** from the appropriate practitioner;
- **as part of a written plan of care**.  
For nursing, home health aide, and therapy services, the ordering practitioner must **review the plan every 60 days**. For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances, the rule has its own review requirements. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]

The services included are:

1. **Part-time or intermittent nursing services**;
2. **Home health aide services**;
3. **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place; and
4. **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology/audiology services**.  
Nursing, aide services, and medical supplies/equipment/appliances are described as required home health benefit categories under the section’s coverage parameters; therapy services are optional under this rule. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided at the beneficiary’s **“place of residence.”** [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]

That term **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

except for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is **not required** to provide. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]

The regulation also makes clear that home health services may be provided in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** except:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid pays or could pay for inpatient services including room and board**. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]

It also expressly says **home health services cannot be limited to people who are homebound**. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]

## Short answer

So, in plain terms: federal Medicaid law defines **home health services** as certain nursing, aide, therapy, and medical supply/equipment services furnished under practitioner orders and a written plan of care, and they must be provided in the person’s **residence or another non-institutional setting where normal life activities occur**, not in institutional inpatient settings like hospitals or nursing facilities. [[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)]
